Preference Assessment Protocol

Indirect nomination, trial-based selection (single stimulus, paired stimulus, multiple stimulus with and without replacement, pictorial and verbal variants), and duration-based measures (free operant, single-stimulus engagement) on one shared stimulus list, with a selection guide, method-specific scoring and graphs, and a combined hierarchy. Adds an ecological assessment of the settings where reinforcers will be used, a competing stimulus assessment for automatically maintained behavior, and a monitoring sheet that tracks the hierarchy and each item's effect over time to catch loss of interest before the plan stalls.

Nothing is stored in the browser. Entries live in this open window only until you save a file; close the tab and they are gone. Save to the district drive, not a personal device.

Preference Assessment Protocol
Form PA-1 · Revised September 2026 · Printed
Selection Guide
What a preference assessment does and does not show A preference assessment ranks stimuli by how often the student approaches, selects, or engages with them. It does not show that any stimulus will function as a reinforcer. Highly preferred stimuli identified by direct assessment usually do function as reinforcers (Piazza et al., 1996; Roscoe et al., 1999), and lower-preference stimuli sometimes do, so the hierarchy is a prediction to be confirmed in a reinforcer assessment or in the treatment data, not a finding.

Decision Rules

1. Start with nomination, not with the caregiver's ranking.
Use the indirect sheet to build the stimulus pool. Do not use caregiver or teacher rankings as the hierarchy: staff opinion has corresponded poorly with direct assessment (Green et al., 1988), teacher rankings correlated strongly with direct assessment for only 1 of 9 toddlers (Cote et al., 2007), and a reinforcer survey was about 57% accurate against later reinforcer assessments (Northup, 2000). Structured interviews such as the RAISD improve the pool that goes into direct assessment (Fisher et al., 1996).
2. Can the student scan an array of three or more items and pick one?
Yes: run an MSWO (DeLeon & Iwata, 1996). It produces a hierarchy comparable to paired stimulus in a fraction of the time. Five sessions is the standard; three sessions (brief MSWO) predicted reinforcers in an early-intervention program (Carr et al., 2000) and is adequate for routine use. No, but the student reliably picks between two: run paired stimulus (Fisher et al., 1992). No to both: run single stimulus with approach and engagement recorded (Pace et al., 1985; Hagopian et al., 2001).
3. Does removing an item, or having a choice removed, evoke problem behavior?
Use the free-operant format (Roane et al., 1998): nothing is removed, so it evokes less problem behavior and takes five minutes. Accept that it usually identifies one or two top items rather than a full hierarchy; the top item can dominate the session.
4. Are you comparing edibles with leisure items?
Assess them in separate pools. Edibles tend to displace leisure items when assessed together (DeLeon et al., 1997), which hides usable leisure reinforcers.
5. Is the stimulus hard to present as an object (activities, outings, social interactions, long videos)?
Use pictorial or verbal presentation only after the prerequisite check below is passed; otherwise pictorial and tangible hierarchies can differ and pictorial high-preference items may not function as reinforcers (Clevenger & Graff, 2005). Deliver the pictured item after each selection: without that contingent access the pictorial format was successful with only some participants (Heinicke et al., 2016). For social stimuli, Kelly et al. (2014) used photos depicting each form of attention, plus a control card that produced no consequence, and checked the resulting hierarchy in a reinforcer assessment.
6. Where will the reinforcer be used, and what will it compete with there?
Complete the Ecological sheet: inventory the settings and routines, mark where each stimulus can be delivered, rate its practical attributes, and observe what the student approaches in real settings. In a preliminary study, free access to the reinforcer after sessions was generally associated with less responding than session-only access (Roane, Call, & Falcomata, 2005); restrict access rather than drop the item.
7. Is the target behavior hypothesized to be automatically maintained?
Add a competing stimulus assessment (Piazza et al., 1998, 2000): a stimulus that the student engages with and that reduces the behavior below its control level is a competing item; a stimulus that is merely preferred is not.
8. Are results ambiguous, tied, or contradicted by the treatment data?
Add a duration-based measure (DeLeon et al., 1999; Kodak et al., 2009) or run a reinforcer assessment. Reassess on a schedule: preferences stay stable for some individuals and shift for others over months (Zhou et al., 2001; Hanley et al., 2006; Ciccone et al., 2007), and on days when a brief MSWO run before work sessions disagreed with the pretreatment assessment, its top item generally drew more responding (DeLeon et al., 2001). The Monitoring sheet logs each brief MSWO and each use of an item, and flags rising latency to approach, falling engagement, rejections, and staff-noted signs before the hierarchy itself changes; reinforcers lose their effectiveness when they are presented repeatedly (Murphy et al., 2003).

Procedural Rules That Apply to Every Direct Method

  • Pre-exposure. Present each stimulus once for the access duration before assessment so that novelty does not drive the first selections.
  • Access. Deliver the selected item for the access duration set in the toolbar (30 s is standard for leisure; edibles are consumed). Do not deliver praise or attention with the item unless attention is a stimulus being assessed.
  • Positioning. Present items about equidistant from the student and rotate positions so that no item is always on the same side. Record side bias on the paired-stimulus sheet.
  • Selection response. Define it before the first trial (touching, reaching within 5 s, pointing, eye gaze for students without hand use). If the student reaches for two items, block both and re-present. If there is no selection within 30 s, score no selection and end the trial or session as the method specifies.
  • Problem behavior. Mark it on every trial where it occurs. A method that produces problem behavior on removal should be replaced with free operant or with shorter access.
  • Interobserver agreement. Collect IOA on at least one session per method when the hierarchy will be written into a plan.
  • Separate pools. Edibles, leisure items, and social interactions are assessed in separate pools of 5–8 stimuli each.

Running an Assessment at the Table

Applied guidance. The single-stimulus, paired-stimulus, MSWO / MSW, free-operant, competing-stimulus and ecological sheets each open with a Run This Assessment panel. It keeps the order the sheet uses, times the response window and the access period (or the session), alerts you when each ends, and writes each trial or session into the sheet’s own fields, so the hierarchy and the percentages update as if the entry had been typed. The panels never print, and nothing in them is saved except what they write into the sheet. The windows and the access period come from this protocol and the toolbar; where the protocol gives none, the panel starts from an editable default.

  • Single stimulus. Each item is presented the set number of times, one block per trial column, each block starting one item further along the pool so no item is always first. Start trial opens the 5-s approach window; Approached starts the access period and times engagement (tap Engaged off when the student disengages, on when engagement resumes); No approach and Rejected end the trial; with no response in the window the trial is scored N.
  • Paired stimulus. Generate the trial list first; the panel presents it in order with its sides. Left or Right starts the access period for that item; with no selection in 30 s the trial is scored Neither. Both means block the reach and present the same pair again as a new trial: the pair’s row records the outcome of that re-presentation, and the panel reports how many times Both was blocked.
  • MSWO / MSW. Set out the array in the order shown and tap the item chosen. After the access period (or Done early, for an edible consumed quickly), the panel removes the item (MSWO) or returns it (MSW), moves the item at the left end to the right end, and shows the new order. No selection in 30 s ends the session. Each session starts one position further along the pool than the last, and each trial goes into that session’s column.
  • Free operant and single-stimulus engagement. In a free-operant session, tap the item the student is engaged with and None when the student is engaged with nothing; choose Several at once when the student can engage with two items together. The seconds for every item, including 0, go into the session’s column. Single-stimulus engagement presents each item alone for the set time, twice in rotated order, with Engaged on and off.
  • Competing stimulus. Run the two control sessions first, then each item for two sessions. Tap Target behavior at each occurrence and Engaged on and off; at the end the panel converts both to the percentage of intervals with the behavior or with engagement (partial interval, at the interval size on the sheet) and writes them into the row.
  • Ecological, in-context observation. During free time, tap the item the student approaches (or type an activity under Not in pool); Approach over stops the time, and Save writes one row with the date, setting, seconds and who initiated. Tapping the next item saves the last one first.
  • Save, discard and pause. Save and next writes the finished trial or session and moves on; Discard writes nothing, so the trial can be run again. Pause stops every clock, for example when the student leaves the table. The runner always works on the first empty cell in its order, so a trial can be run again by clearing its cell. A blank date on the sheet is filled when you start.
  • Alerts and keys. Each end of a window, access period or session sounds a tone, flashes the edge of the screen and, on a phone or tablet, vibrates; each can be turned off, and Test alert plays one. The screen is kept awake while a runner is running. One runner runs at a time: the pool size, the settings it uses and Load simulation, Open data and Clear all are locked until it ends, and a button in the corner leads back to it from any other sheet. Each panel lists its keyboard keys.

Prerequisite Check for Pictorial or Verbal Formats

Before any pictorial or verbal variant, run 10 picture–object (or word–object) matching trials: place three objects, present a picture (or say the name), and ask the student to match or hand over the corresponding object; then reverse (object to picture). Clevenger and Graff (2005) tested both directions (eight trials each, three-item comparison array) and suggested that both may be prerequisites for pictorial assessment. The trial count and pass criterion below are working conventions for this practice.

DirectionTrial outcomes (tap to toggle: + correct, − error, blank not run)Correct% correctPassed (≥ 90%)
Decision rules synthesize the practitioner models of Karsten, Carr, and Lepper (2011) and Virués-Ortega et al. (2014) and the reviews by Kang et al. (2013) and Tullis et al. (2011). Time estimates are approximate and depend on access duration, array size, and the student's latency to select. Full references are on the summary sheet.

Structured Informant Interview (After the RAISD; Fisher et al., 1996)

Ask the informant for specific items or events in each category, then how the student behaves when each is present or removed. Record names of specific stimuli, not categories. Informant:

Stimulus Pool for Direct Assessment

Enter the stimuli chosen for direct assessment; this list feeds every other sheet. Set the number of stimuli in the toolbar (5–8 is typical; MSWO arrays above 7–8 become unwieldy). The informant's rank is recorded for comparison only.

#Stimulus (exact form presented)TypeSource of nominationInformant rankNotes (portion, model, access rule)
Interview categories follow the Reinforcer Assessment for Individuals with Severe Disabilities (Fisher, Piazza, Bowman, & Amari, 1996, American Journal on Mental Retardation, 101, 15–25), in which stimuli nominated through the structured interview and then assessed directly were more effective reinforcers than those from a standard list. Green et al. (1988, JABA, 21, 31–43) found staff opinion a poor predictor of assessed preference; Northup (2000, JABA, 33, 335–338) found a reinforcer survey about 57% accurate against concurrent-operants reinforcer assessments with 20 children with attention deficit disorders; in the study it replicated, survey results often rated multiple categories as high preference and were less likely to identify low-preference categories (Northup et al., 1996); Cote et al. (2007, JABA, 40, 157–166) found a strong teacher–assessment correlation for only 1 of 9 toddlers; the top items from both methods functioned as reinforcers, and the direct assessment's top item was the more effective reinforcer for 5 of the 9.

Keys: Space start trial, pause or resume · A approached · N no approach · R rejected · E engaged on or off · D done early · X problem behavior · S or Enter save and next.
Procedure Present one stimulus at a time, within reach, for up to 5 s. Score A if the student approaches (touches, reaches, orients toward) within 5 s, N if there is no approach, and R if the student rejects it (pushes away, turns away, negative vocalization). On approach, allow access for the set duration and record seconds engaged. Present each item the set number of times in a rotated order so that no item is always first. Trials per item and access duration are set in the toolbar.

Single-Stimulus Hierarchy

RankStimulusTrials% approachMean engagement (s)% engagementPB trialsCategory

Category bands (working convention for this practice, applied to % approach): HP ≥ 80%, MP 40–79%, LP < 40%. Where several items reach 100% approach (the pattern Fisher et al., 1992, reported for the single-stimulus format), rank them by % engagement; DeLeon et al. (1999) resolved ambiguous approach results with a duration-based measure.

Single-stimulus approach method after Pace, Ivancic, Edwards, Iwata, and Page (1985, JABA, 18, 249–255). Fisher et al. (1992) found the format produced many items approached on nearly every trial, so it failed to differentiate among high-preference items; the engagement measure follows Hagopian, Rush, Lewin, and Long (2001, JABA, 34, 475–485), who showed single-stimulus engagement predicted reinforcer effects. The format remains the choice for students who do not make a selection response between two items.

Keys: Space start trial, pause or resume · L or ← left · R or → right · N neither · B both · D done early · X problem behavior · S or Enter save and next.
Procedure Every stimulus is paired with every other stimulus. Present the pair, one item on each side, and prompt "pick one." Score which side was selected, Neither if no selection within 30 s (remove both), or Both if the student reached for both (block and re-present; the re-presentation is a new trial). Deliver the selected item for the access duration and remove the other. The trial list below is generated from the stimulus pool with sides counterbalanced and order shuffled; use the seed to reproduce a list.

Paired-Stimulus Hierarchy

RankStimulusPresentedSelected% selectedPB trialsCategory

Category bands (working convention): HP ≥ 80% of presentations selected, MP 40–79%, LP < 40%. A side bias above about 75% of selections to one side means the hierarchy reflects position, not preference; re-run with the selection response prompted to the array center or use MSWO with rotated positions.

Paired-stimulus method after Fisher, Piazza, Bowman, Hagopian, Owens, and Slevin (1992, JABA, 25, 491–498), who found it produced greater differentiation than the single-stimulus format and that items ranked higher in the paired format were more effective reinforcers. DeLeon and Iwata (1996) obtained comparable hierarchies from MSWO in less time. Verriden and Roscoe (2016, JABA, 49, 265–285) compared four methods across repeated administrations and found the most stable rankings with paired stimulus and MSWO, lower stability with free operant and response restriction, and consistently lower problem behavior with free operant.

MSWO after DeLeon and Iwata (1996, JABA, 29, 519–533), who scored each stimulus as the percentage of trials in which it was selected out of trials in which it was available and found MSWO hierarchies comparable to paired stimulus with fewer trials, while MSW (Windsor, Piché, & Locke, 1994, Research in Developmental Disabilities, 15, 439–455) identified fewer stimuli because the top item could be selected repeatedly. The three-session brief MSWO is from Carr, Nicolson, and Higbee (2000, JABA, 33, 353–357). Daily brief MSWO before sessions follows DeLeon et al. (2001, JABA, 34, 463–473).

A. Free-Operant Assessment

Procedure Place all stimuli in the pool within reach at once. Say "you can play with anything here," then withhold prompts and attention for the session (5 min standard; set in the toolbar). Record seconds engaged with each item (continuous duration, or 10-s partial-interval counts converted to seconds). Nothing is removed, so engagement with two items at once is possible and item percentages need not sum to 100. Run 1–3 sessions.

B. Single-Stimulus Engagement (Duration)

Procedure Present one stimulus at a time for the duration set in the toolbar (2 min standard). Record seconds engaged. Present each item twice in rotated order. Use for leisure items when the student does not make selection responses, or to break ties from a selection-based assessment.

Duration-Based Hierarchy

RankStimulusFO sessionsFO mean % engagedSS-duration presentationsSS-duration % engagedCategory

Category bands (working convention, applied to whichever duration measure was run): HP ≥ 50% of session engaged, MP 20–49%, LP < 20%. These are not comparable to selection percentages. If one item consumes most of the free-operant session, treat the rest of that hierarchy as unassessed and run single-stimulus engagement or MSWO for the remaining items.

Free-operant method after Roane, Vollmer, Ringdahl, and Marcus (1998, JABA, 31, 605–620): shorter than paired stimulus and associated with less problem behavior, but it identified fewer differentiated stimuli. Duration-based single-stimulus measures after DeLeon, Iwata, Conners, and Wallace (1999, JABA, 32, 111–114) and Hagopian et al. (2001). Kodak, Fisher, Kelley, and Kisamore (2009, Research in Developmental Disabilities, 30, 1068–1077) compared a selection-based (multiple-stimulus with replacement) and a duration-based (free-operant) assessment with four participants: the top-ranked item differed between the two for every participant, and the MSW's top item was the most effective reinforcer for two of the four. Response-restriction analysis (Hanley, Iwata, Lindberg, & Conners, 2003, JABA, 36, 47–58), in which the top free-operant item is withdrawn and the session repeated, converts the free-operant format into a full hierarchy when needed.

Alerts:
Keys: 1–9 start timing the item approached · O or Space approach over · P pause or resume · S or Enter save.
Purpose A hierarchy tells you what the student prefers under assessment conditions; it does not tell you whether the item can be delivered in the settings where the plan runs, what it will compete with there, or whether the student already has free access to it. This sheet inventories the settings and routines (after the ecological-inventory strategy of Brown et al., 1979), records where each stimulus can be delivered and its practical attributes, and adds a naturalistic observation of what the student approaches in real settings. The contextual-fit score joins the preference rank on the Summary sheet; a highly preferred item with poor fit is a candidate for a restricted-access (closed-economy) arrangement rather than for exclusion.

A. Settings and Routines Inventory

One row per setting or routine in which the plan will operate. Name the reinforcers the environment already provides, the choice opportunities that exist, and the stimuli that will compete with anything the plan delivers.

Setting / routineTimeStaff (ratio)Reinforcers naturally availableChoice opportunitiesCompeting stimuli presentDemand level

B. Where Each Stimulus Can Be Delivered

Y deliverable as assessed; A deliverable with adaptation (smaller portion, shorter access, headphones, staff carries it); N not deliverable in that setting.

C. Practical Attributes of Each Stimulus

StimulusPortableAccess / consumption timeSatiation riskStaff neededAge-appropriateInterferes with instructionFree access outside sessionsFit

Fit score (working convention for this practice): one point each for portable, brief access, low satiation risk, no extra staff, age-appropriate, no interference, and no free access outside sessions; half a point for the intermediate ratings; reported as a percentage of 7. Good ≥ 75%, Fair 50–74%, Poor < 50%. "Free access outside sessions" is scored against the item because free access to a reinforcer after sessions was generally associated with less responding than session-only access (Roane, Call, & Falcomata, 2005); the remedy is to restrict access, not to drop the item.

D. In-Context Observation of Preference

During free time in natural settings, with no prompts, record each item or activity the student approaches, how long they stay with it, and who initiated. Items not in the pool are written in and counted separately; they are candidates for the next pool.

DateSettingItem / activity in poolNot in pool (write in)Duration (s)Initiated byNotes
Settings inventory after the ecological-inventory strategy of Brown, Branston, Hamre-Nietupski, Pumpian, Certo, and Gruenewald (1979, Journal of Special Education, 13, 81–90) and the contextual-fit framework of Albin, Lucyshyn, Horner, and Flannery (1996). Open- versus closed-economy effects on responding after Roane, Call, and Falcomata (2005, JABA, 38, 335–348); motivating-operation effects on reinforcer effectiveness after Vollmer and Iwata (1991, JABA, 24, 279–291). In-context observation adapts to natural settings the free-operant format of Roane et al. (1998) and Ortiz and Carr (2000, Behavioral Interventions, 15, 345–353); choice-making as an intervention after Kern et al. (1998, Journal of Behavioral Education, 8, 151–169). The fit score is this form's convention and has no empirical validation.

Competing Stimulus Assessment (Automatically Maintained Behavior)

Date / assessor

Times each control or stimulus session, counts the target behavior, times engagement with the item, and writes the percentages of intervals into the table below.
Session length300 sfrom the sheet
Intervals10 sfrom the sheet
Control session 1
Control (no items)
Session
5:00
Alerts:
Keys: Space start, pause or resume · X target behavior · E engaged on or off · Z undo the last target behavior · S or Enter save and next.
Procedure Use when the target behavior is hypothesized (EA-1) to be automatically maintained. Run two control sessions with no items available and record the percentage of 10-s intervals with the target behavior. Then present each stimulus alone for two sessions of the same length (5 min is this form's default; published assessments have sampled 30 s to 10 min, DeLeon et al., 2005) and record the percentage of intervals with engagement and the percentage with the target behavior. Deliver no attention and no other consequences during any session. A stimulus competes when the student engages with it and the target behavior falls well below its control level; items that produce high engagement without reducing the behavior are preferred but not competing.

Category (working convention for this practice): Competing when mean engagement ≥ 50% of intervals and the target behavior is reduced by ≥ 80% from the control mean; Partly competing when engagement ≥ 50% and the reduction is 50–79%; otherwise Not competing. A control mean below 20% of intervals makes reductions hard to detect; extend the control sessions or run the assessment when the behavior is more likely.

Competing stimulus assessment after Piazza, Fisher, Hanley, LeBlanc, Worsdell, Lindauer, and Keeney (1998, JABA, 31, 165–189) and Piazza, Adelinis, Hanley, Goh, and Delia (2000, JABA, 33, 13–27), who identified stimuli that both produced engagement and reduced automatically maintained behavior. Haddock and Hagopian (2020, JABA, 53, 1982–2001) reviewed the method and its criteria; Hagopian, Rooker, and Zarcone (2015, JABA, 48, 523–543) describe subtypes of automatically maintained self-injury that differ in response to competing stimuli. The 50% / 80% criteria are this form's conventions.

Monitoring Preference and Reinforcer Effectiveness over Time

See it at the table in the walkthrough →

Student
Pool
Monitoring since
Why monitor Preferences stay stable for some individuals and shift for others over months (Zhou, Iwata, Goff, & Shore, 2001; Hanley, Iwata, & Roscoe, 2006), and reinforcer effectiveness and preference shift with satiation and deprivation (Vollmer & Iwata, 1991; Gottschalk, Libby, & Graff, 2000; McAdam et al., 2005). Murphy, McSweeney, Smith, and McComas (2003) note that reinforcers lose their effectiveness when they are presented repeatedly and argue that habituation describes this better than satiation and gives specific guidance on maintaining a reinforcer's effectiveness. The earliest signs are not in the hierarchy; they are in the student's behavior toward the item: longer latency to approach or select it, shorter engagement once it is delivered, lower response rates under the schedule, rejections, and shifts toward other items. Two logs below capture both: a brief MSWO log tracks the hierarchy, and a reinforcer-use log tracks the item's effect each time it is used.

A. Brief MSWO Log (Top Three by Date)

Record the top three from each brief (three-session) MSWO. Daily before sessions for edibles, weekly or at plan review for leisure items. The graph plots each item's rank across dates; an item that falls off the top three or a new item entering it is a shift.

Date#1#2#3SessionsPBNote (MO, time since meal or last access, setting)

B. Reinforcer-Use Log (Signs of Waning Effectiveness)

One row each time an item from the hierarchy is used as a reinforcer in a session or in the classroom. Latency is seconds from offer to approach or selection; engagement is seconds with the item out of the access period; responses per minute is the rate of the target response under the schedule, if measured. Signs are what staff saw when the item was delivered.

DateItemContextLatency (s)Engaged (s)Resp / minRejectedSignsNote

C. Decision Rules for a Shift

  • Check the motivating operation first. A slow approach after a meal, after free access at home, or late in a long session may be a satiation effect rather than a preference change: response rates for food were lower after meals than before them for 4 of 9 adults (Zhou, Iwata, & Shore, 2002), and free access to an item just before assessment reduced preference for it (Gottschalk, Libby, & Graff, 2000; McAdam et al., 2005). Note time since the last meal or access on the log before concluding anything.
  • Watch. One flag on one item: continue, add the item to the next brief MSWO, and rotate a second high-preference item into the schedule.
  • Shifted. Two or more flags, or the item leaves the top three on two consecutive brief MSWOs: rerun the full assessment for that pool, restrict the item's free access if it has any, and move the plan to the current top item. Do not remove the item from the pool: in Hanley et al. (2006), an item whose rank fell during extended daily access regained rank once that access ended, fully for one participant and partly for the other.
  • Effect in doubt. If the hierarchy is stable but response rates under the schedule fall, the problem is the schedule or the response effort, not the item: run RA-1 (progressive-ratio) on the top two items before changing the plan.
  • Habituation. Signs that appear within a session and disappear after a break point to habituation; vary the item across deliveries or alternate two items rather than replacing either (Murphy et al., 2003).
Preference stability after Zhou et al. (2001, JABA, 34, 179–184), Ciccone, Graff, and Ahearn (2007), and Hanley, Iwata, and Roscoe (2006, JABA, 39, 189–202). Motivating-operation effects after Vollmer and Iwata (1991), Gottschalk, Libby, and Graff (2000, JABA, 33, 85–88), Zhou, Iwata, and Shore (2002, JABA, 35, 411–414), and McAdam, Klatt, Koffarnus, Dicesare, Solberg, Welch, and Murphy (2005, JABA, 38, 107–110). Habituation and dynamic reinforcer effectiveness after Murphy, McSweeney, Smith, and McComas (2003, JABA, 36, 421–438). The daily brief MSWO follows DeLeon et al. (2001). The flag thresholds below the graphs are working conventions for this practice.

Walkthrough: Running the Preference Assessments at the Table

What each part of the protocol looks like at the table: the therapist, the student and the data collector drawn step by step, what is said, what the student does, what the sheet’s Run This Assessment panel shows, and what goes on the sheet. The items are the form’s own simulated pools. The words and the numbers follow the form’s own sheets, and each method’s procedure is quoted word for word. Press Play all in any section to watch it run, then try the practice at the end.

S Before any assessmentA Single stimulusB Paired stimulusC MSWOD Free operant and durationE EcologicalF Competing stimulusG Reading the summaryH Monitoring over timePracticeTerms

S. Before Any Assessment

Indirect & stimulus pool · the Guide’s procedural rules · the toolbar

The pool comes from nomination, the pools are kept apart, and the rules that apply to every direct method are settled before the first trial: the selection response, pre-exposure, positions, access, and who records.

    TherapistStudentData collectorSecond observerThe Run This Assessment panel, drawn largeFrom above: the table as the student sits at itThe item selected

    What You Say and Do

    • Interview for specific stimuli in each category, not categories; build the pool from the nominations.
    • Keep edibles, leisure items and social interactions in separate pools; before an edible pool, read the Restrictions line.
    • Before the first trial: the selection response defined, each stimulus presented once for the access duration, positions about equidistant and rotated.
    • Deliver each selected item for the access duration without praise or attention.

    What Goes on the Sheet

    • Indirect & stimulus pool: Purpose of assessment, Pool being assessed, Selection response, Restrictions (allergies, diet, safety, school policy), the interview, and the pool: Stimulus (exact form presented), Type, Source of nomination, Informant rank, Notes.
    • The toolbar: Stimuli in pool, Access per trial (s), SS trials / item, PS presentations, Multiple-stimulus format and sessions, FO session (s) / SS-duration (s).
    • For a pictorial or verbal format: the Prerequisite Check on the Guide, and Format cleared for use.
    Why. Staff opinion has corresponded poorly with direct assessment (Green et al., 1988); teacher rankings correlated strongly with direct assessment for only 1 of 9 toddlers (Cote et al., 2007), and a reinforcer survey was about 57% accurate against later reinforcer assessments (Northup, 2000). So the informant nominates and the direct assessment ranks. The rules below keep novelty, position and attention from deciding the selections.

    The Guide’s Rules for Every Direct Method, Word for Word

    Pre-exposurePresent each stimulus once for the access duration before assessment so that novelty does not drive the first selections.
    AccessDeliver the selected item for the access duration set in the toolbar (30 s is standard for leisure; edibles are consumed). Do not deliver praise or attention with the item unless attention is a stimulus being assessed.
    PositioningPresent items about equidistant from the student and rotate positions so that no item is always on the same side. Record side bias on the paired-stimulus sheet.
    Selection responseDefine it before the first trial (touching, reaching within 5 s, pointing, eye gaze for students without hand use). If the student reaches for two items, block both and re-present.
    Problem behaviorMark it on every trial where it occurs. A method that produces problem behavior on removal should be replaced with free operant or with shorter access.
    Interobserver agreementCollect IOA on at least one session per method when the hierarchy will be written into a plan.
    Separate poolsEdibles, leisure items, and social interactions are assessed in separate pools of 5–8 stimuli each.

    A. Single Stimulus

    Single stimulus · approach within 5 s, then access · for students who do not select between two items

    One item at a time: the student approaches it, does not, or rejects it, and an approach earns the access period, with the seconds engaged recorded. It is the format for a student who does not make a selection response between two items.

      What You Say and Do

      • Present the item the panel names, within reach, and press Start trial: the 5-s approach window runs.
      • Tap Approached, No approach or Rejected. An approach starts the access period, with no praise or attention; tap Engaged off when the student disengages and on when engagement resumes.
      • Problem behavior during the trial: tap Problem behavior. Save and next writes the trial and names the next item.

      What Goes on the Sheet

      • Save and next writes each trial into its column: A / N / R, and on an approach the seconds engaged (sec).
      • PB: the item’s trials with problem behavior, counted up by the panel.
      • The Single-Stimulus Hierarchy computes % approach, Mean engagement (s), % engagement and the Category.
      Decision. Categories come from % approach: HP ≥ 80%, MP 40–79%, LP < 40% (working conventions). Where several items reach 100% approach, rank them by % engagement: Fisher et al. (1992) found this format failed to differentiate among high-preference items, and single-stimulus engagement predicted reinforcer effects (Hagopian et al., 2001).

      The Sheet’s Procedure, Word for Word

      Single stimulusPresent one stimulus at a time, within reach, for up to 5 s. Score A if the student approaches (touches, reaches, orients toward) within 5 s, N if there is no approach, and R if the student rejects it (pushes away, turns away, negative vocalization). On approach, allow access for the set duration and record seconds engaged. Present each item the set number of times in a rotated order so that no item is always first. Trials per item and access duration are set in the toolbar.

      B. Paired Stimulus

      Paired stimulus · every pair, sides counterbalanced · Left, Right, Neither, Both

      Two items at a time, every stimulus against every other, with sides counterbalanced: more differentiated than single stimulus and a better predictor of reinforcer effects (Fisher et al., 1992), but slow.

        What You Say and Do

        • Place the pair as the panel shows it, one item on each side, say “pick one,” and press Start trial: the 30-s response window runs.
        • Tap Left or Right: the selected item for the access period, the other removed. No selection within 30 s: Neither, both removed. A reach for both: block both, tap Both, and present the same pair again.
        • Decide whose left and right the list means before the first trial, and keep it for every trial.

        What Goes on the Sheet

        • Seed, then Generate trial list. Save and next writes each trial’s Selected: Left, Right or Neither; with the panel, a pair presented again after Both takes the outcome of the re-presentation, and scored by hand the row reads Both. PB when problem behavior occurred on that trial.
        • The Paired-Stimulus Hierarchy computes Presented, Selected, % selected and the Category, with Left selections, Right selections, Side bias and No selection.
        Decision. HP ≥ 80% of presentations selected, MP 40–79%, LP < 40% (working conventions). A side bias above about 75% of selections to one side means the hierarchy reflects position, not preference: re-run with the selection response prompted to the array center, or use MSWO with rotated positions.

        The Sheet’s Procedure, Word for Word

        Paired stimulusEvery stimulus is paired with every other stimulus. Present the pair, one item on each side, and prompt “pick one.” Score which side was selected, Neither if no selection within 30 s (remove both), or Both if the student reached for both (block and re-present; the re-presentation is a new trial). Deliver the selected item for the access duration and remove the other. The trial list below is generated from the stimulus pool with sides counterbalanced and order shuffled; use the seed to reproduce a list.

        C. Multiple Stimulus Without Replacement (MSWO)

        MSWO / MSW · select, access, remove, rotate · five sessions, three for a brief MSWO

        The whole pool in a line. Each selection is removed for the rest of the session and the remaining items are rotated one position, until every item is chosen or 30 s pass with no selection.

          What You Say and Do

          • Set the array out in the order the panel shows, in a line, equidistant from the student; “pick one,” and Start trial.
          • Tap the item chosen. Access for 30 s, or Done early when an edible is consumed; the selected item does not return this session.
          • Save and next: the panel moves the item at the left end to the right end and shows the new order. No selection within 30 s ends the session.

          What Goes on the Sheet

          • For each session, the item chosen at each trial, or No selection at the trial that ended the session, written by Save and next.
          • PB in session, checked when Problem behavior was tapped in that session.
          • The MSWO hierarchy computes Times available, Times selected, % selected, Mean position and the Category.
          Decision. % selected = times selected ÷ times available × 100 (DeLeon & Iwata, 1996). HP ≥ 80%, MP 40–79%, LP < 40% (working conventions). MSWO gives a hierarchy comparable to paired stimulus with far fewer trials; with replacement (MSW) the top item can be chosen every time, so MSW identifies the top item but little else.

          The Sheet’s Procedure, Word for Word

          MSWO, with 6 stimuli, 30-s access and 5 sessions set in the toolbarPlace all 6 stimuli in a line, equidistant from the student, and prompt “pick one.” Give access for 30 s (or until consumed), then remove the selected item, rotate the remaining items one position, and re-present. Continue until every item is selected or no selection occurs within 30 s, which ends the session. Record the item chosen at each trial position. Run 5 sessions (five is standard; three for a brief MSWO).

          D. Free Operant and Single-Stimulus Engagement

          Free operant & duration · seconds engaged, nothing removed · one item at a time for 2 min

          Duration instead of selection. In free operant the whole pool is available for a session and nothing is removed, so it evokes less problem behavior; single-stimulus engagement presents one item at a time.

            What You Say and Do

            • Free operant: every item within reach; “you can play with anything here”; Start session; then no prompts and no attention for the session.
            • Nothing is removed. Tap the item the student is with, and None when the student is with nothing; Several at once times two items together.
            • Single-stimulus engagement: one item for the set duration, each item twice, in rotated order; Start presentation, then Engaged on and off.

            What Goes on the Sheet

            • Engagement definition first.
            • A. Free-Operant Assessment: Save and next writes each item’s Session 1 (s), Session 2 (s) or Session 3 (s); Mean % is computed.
            • B. Single-Stimulus Engagement: Presentation 1 (s), Presentation 2 (s).
            • The Duration-Based Hierarchy computes both measures and the Category.
            Decision. HP ≥ 50% of the session engaged, MP 20–49%, LP < 20% (working conventions), not comparable to selection percentages. Free operant usually identifies one or two top items rather than a full hierarchy. If one item consumes most of the session, the rest is unassessed: run single-stimulus engagement or MSWO for the remaining items, or a response-restriction analysis, in which the top item is withdrawn and the session repeated (Hanley et al., 2003).

            The Sheet’s Procedures, Word for Word

            A. Free-operant assessmentPlace all stimuli in the pool within reach at once. Say “you can play with anything here,” then withhold prompts and attention for the session (5 min standard; set in the toolbar). Record seconds engaged with each item (continuous duration, or 10-s partial-interval counts converted to seconds). Nothing is removed, so engagement with two items at once is possible and item percentages need not sum to 100. Run 1–3 sessions.
            B. Single-stimulus engagement (duration)Present one stimulus at a time for the duration set in the toolbar (2 min standard). Record seconds engaged. Present each item twice in rotated order. Use for leisure items when the student does not make selection responses, or to break ties from a selection-based assessment.

            E. Ecological Assessment

            Ecological · settings, deliverability, practical attributes · in-context observation

            Whether an item can be delivered in the settings where the plan runs, what it competes with there, and whether the student already has free access to it; then what the student approaches in real settings.

              What You Say and Do

              • List each setting or routine the plan will run in, with what is already available, the choices, the competition and the demand.
              • Rate each stimulus in each setting (Y, A or N), then its practical attributes.
              • Observe free time in natural settings with no prompts. On the panel: Start observation; tap the item approached, or type an activity under Not in pool (write in) and press Time this one; Approach over when the student leaves it; Save; End observation when free time ends.

              What Goes on the Sheet

              • A. Settings and Routines Inventory; B. Where Each Stimulus Can Be Delivered (Usable is counted).
              • C. Practical Attributes of Each Stimulus; the Fit is computed and joins the Summary.
              • D. In-Context Observation: Date, Setting, Item / activity in pool or Not in pool (write in), Duration (s), Initiated by, Notes.
              Decision. A highly preferred item with poor fit is a candidate for a restricted-access (closed-economy) arrangement rather than for exclusion: in a preliminary study, free access to the reinforcer after sessions was generally associated with less responding than session-only access (Roane, Call, & Falcomata, 2005). Items approached outside the pool are candidates for the next pool. The fit score is this form’s convention and has no empirical validation.

              The Sheet’s Procedure, Word for Word

              D. In-context observation of preferenceDuring free time in natural settings, with no prompts, record each item or activity the student approaches, how long they stay with it, and who initiated. Items not in the pool are written in and counted separately; they are candidates for the next pool.

              F. Competing Stimulus Assessment

              Competing stimulus · for behavior hypothesized to be automatically maintained · control sessions, then each item alone

              Not which item the student prefers, but which item competes with automatically maintained behavior: engagement with it, and the target behavior well below its control level.

                What You Say and Do

                • Two control sessions with no items; then each item alone for two sessions of the same length. On the panel: Condition and Session, then Start session.
                • No attention and no other consequences in any session.
                • Tap Target behavior at each occurrence (Undo takes back the last) and Engaged on and off; the panel converts both to the percentage of 10-s intervals.

                What Goes on the Sheet

                • Target behavior, Session length (s), Interval size, Hypothesis source.
                • Save and next writes Control (no items): Ses 1 % PB and Ses 2 % PB; for each item Ses 1 % eng, Ses 1 % PB, Ses 2 % eng, Ses 2 % PB.
                • Mean eng, Mean PB, PB vs control and the Category are computed.
                Decision. Competing when mean engagement is at least 50% of intervals and the target behavior is reduced by at least 80% from the control mean; Partly competing at 50–79%; otherwise Not competing (this form’s conventions). A control mean below 20% of intervals makes reductions hard to detect: extend the control sessions, or run the assessment when the behavior is more likely.

                The Sheet’s Procedure, Word for Word

                Competing stimulus assessmentUse when the target behavior is hypothesized (EA-1) to be automatically maintained. Run two control sessions with no items available and record the percentage of 10-s intervals with the target behavior. Then present each stimulus alone for two sessions of the same length (…) and record the percentage of intervals with engagement and the percentage with the target behavior. Deliver no attention and no other consequences during any session. A stimulus competes when the student engages with it and the target behavior falls well below its control level; items that produce high engagement without reducing the behavior are preferred but not competing.

                G. Reading the Summary

                Summary · the combined hierarchy, the categories, agreement between methods, fit · a worked example you can enter yourself

                The Summary puts every method completed side by side. The numbers here are what the form computes for a worked example of the six leisure items: paired stimulus, MSWO and free operant.

                  What You Say and Do

                  • Compare methods by rank, never by value across selection and duration.
                  • Read each row for agreement; plan a reinforcer assessment for a stimulus the methods disagree on.
                  • Read the Fit column before recommending an item, and write its access rule.

                  What Goes on the Sheet

                  • Interobserver agreement (method, sessions, %), Problem behavior across methods (summary), Reinforcer assessment planned (design, stimuli, response), Reassessment schedule.
                  • Stimuli recommended for the plan (with access rules), Stimuli to keep out of the plan and why, Limitations of this assessment.
                  • Interobserver Agreement by Method; the signatures.
                  Decision. A preference assessment ranks stimuli; it does not show that any of them will function as a reinforcer. The hierarchy is a prediction, confirmed in a reinforcer assessment or in the treatment data. Composite categories are working conventions: HP within the top third of the pool, MP the middle third, LP the bottom third.

                  To see these numbers on the form, enter the six items as the pool (Tablet (video), Bubbles, Squeeze ball, Picture book, Musical toy, Blocks; informant ranks 1, 3, 5, 6, 2, 4). Paired stimulus: seed 1, each pair once, the student choosing in each pair the item earlier in the order Tablet (video), Bubbles, Squeeze ball, Musical toy, Picture book, Blocks, except trial 3 (Blocks and Picture book), scored Neither. MSWO, five sessions: session 1 in that same order; session 2 Tablet (video), Squeeze ball, Bubbles, Musical toy, Blocks, Picture book; session 3 Bubbles, Tablet (video), Squeeze ball, Picture book, Musical toy, Blocks; session 4 Tablet (video), Bubbles, Musical toy, Squeeze ball, Picture book, No selection; session 5 as session 1. Free operant, two sessions (s), in pool order: 150 and 160; 60 and 70; 40 and 50; 10 and 20; 90 and 70; 10 and 0.

                  H. Monitoring Preference over Time

                  Monitoring · the brief MSWO log and the reinforcer-use log · Decision Rules for a Shift

                  Preferences stay stable for some individuals and shift for others over months, and reinforcer effectiveness and preference shift with satiation and deprivation. The earliest signs are not in the hierarchy; they are in the student’s behavior toward the item.

                    What You Say and Do

                    • A brief MSWO (three sessions) daily before sessions for edibles, weekly or at plan review for leisure items.
                    • Each time an item is used as a reinforcer, time the latency from the offer and the seconds engaged, and note what you saw.
                    • Before reading a slow approach as a change, note the time since the last meal or access.

                    What Goes on the Sheet

                    • A. Brief MSWO Log: Date, #1, #2, #3, Sessions, PB, Note (MO, time since meal or last access, setting).
                    • B. Reinforcer-Use Log: Date, Item, Context, Latency (s), Engaged (s), Resp / min, Rejected, Signs, Note.
                    • Graph item picks the item the graphs and the verdict show.
                    Decision. Check the motivating operation first. One flag on one item is Watch; two or more flags, or the item out of the top three on two consecutive brief MSWOs, is Shifted. A stable hierarchy with falling response rates points to the schedule or the response effort, not the item. The flag thresholds are working conventions for this practice.

                    The Sheet’s Decision Rules for a Shift, Word for Word

                    Check the motivating operation firstA slow approach after a meal, after free access at home, or late in a long session … Note time since the last meal or access on the log before concluding anything …
                    WatchOne flag on one item: continue, add the item to the next brief MSWO, and rotate a second high-preference item into the schedule.
                    ShiftedTwo or more flags, or the item leaves the top three on two consecutive brief MSWOs: rerun the full assessment for that pool, restrict the item's free access if it has any, and move the plan to the current top item.
                    Effect in doubtIf the hierarchy is stable but response rates under the schedule fall, the problem is the schedule or the response effort, not the item: run RA-1 (progressive-ratio) on the top two items before changing the plan.
                    HabituationSigns that appear within a session and disappear after a break point to habituation; vary the item across deliveries or alternate two items rather than replacing either (Murphy et al., 2003).

                    The item stays in the pool: in Hanley et al. (2006), an item whose rank fell during extended daily access regained rank once that access ended, fully for one participant and partly for the other.

                    Practice: Your Call

                    Moments where trials and readings most often go wrong, drawn as they happen. Pick your call; the rule comes back with the answer.

                    Terms, as the Form Uses Them

                    For the therapist, the data collector and the analyst
                    Stimulus pool
                    The stimuli chosen for direct assessment, entered on the Indirect sheet in the exact form presented. 5–8 is typical; the list feeds every other sheet.
                    Nomination and informant rank
                    The indirect assessment nominates stimuli for the pool. The informant’s rank is recorded for comparison only: staff opinion has corresponded poorly with direct assessment (Green et al., 1988), and teacher rankings correlated strongly with it for only 1 of 9 toddlers (Cote et al., 2007).
                    Separate pools
                    Edibles, leisure items, and social interactions are assessed in separate pools of 5–8 stimuli each; edibles tend to displace leisure items when they are assessed together.
                    Selection response
                    What counts as choosing, defined before the first trial: touching, reaching within 5 s, pointing, or eye gaze for students without hand use.
                    Pre-exposure
                    Each stimulus presented once for the access duration before the assessment, so that novelty does not drive the first selections.
                    Access duration
                    How long the selected item is delivered: Access per trial (s) in the toolbar, 30 s the standard for leisure items; edibles are consumed. No praise or attention comes with the item unless attention is a stimulus being assessed.
                    Approach (A), no approach (N), rejection (R)
                    Single-stimulus scoring: A for touching, reaching, or orienting toward the item within 5 s; N for no approach; R for pushing it away, turning away, or a negative vocalization.
                    % approach and % engagement
                    Single stimulus: the share of an item’s trials scored A, and its mean seconds engaged on those trials as a share of the access period.
                    Paired-stimulus trial list
                    Every stimulus paired with every other, sides counterbalanced and order shuffled from a seed; each pair once, or twice with sides reversed.
                    Left, Right, Neither, Both
                    Left or Right is the side selected. Neither: no selection within 30 s, both items removed. Both: a reach for both, blocked and re-presented, the re-presentation a new trial; a row scored Both is left out of the hierarchy’s counts.
                    Side bias
                    About 75% or more of paired-stimulus selections to one side: the hierarchy then reflects position, not preference.
                    MSWO
                    Multiple stimulus without replacement: the pool in a line; the selected item is removed and the rest rotated one position and re-presented, until every item is selected or 30 s pass with no selection.
                    MSW
                    Multiple stimulus with replacement: the selected item goes back into the array for a fixed number of trials. One or two items tend to dominate, and the rest are not reliably ranked.
                    Times available and % selected
                    In MSWO an item is available on every trial it is in the array; % selected = times selected ÷ times available × 100.
                    Mean position
                    The average MSWO trial at which an item was chosen; lower is more preferred.
                    Brief MSWO
                    Three MSWO sessions, which predicted reinforcers in an early-intervention program (Carr et al., 2000) and are adequate for routine use; the Monitoring sheet logs the top three of each.
                    Free operant
                    The whole pool within reach for a session (5 min standard), prompts and attention withheld, nothing removed; the seconds engaged with each item are recorded.
                    Single-stimulus engagement
                    A duration measure: one item at a time for the set duration (2 min standard), each item twice in rotated order, seconds engaged recorded.
                    HP, MP, LP
                    High, moderate and low preference, by working conventions that differ by sheet: selection percentages HP ≥ 80%, MP 40–79%, LP < 40%; duration HP ≥ 50%, MP 20–49%, LP < 20% of the session; on the Summary, the top, middle and bottom third of the pool.
                    Mean rank and composite
                    On the Summary, the mean of a stimulus’s ranks across the direct methods completed, and its third of the pool. The informant’s rank is not included.
                    Contextual fit
                    The Ecological sheet’s score of an item’s practical attributes, as a percentage of 7: Good ≥ 75%, Fair 50–74%, Poor < 50%. A working convention with no empirical validation.
                    Restricted access (closed economy)
                    The remedy for a preferred item that is freely available elsewhere or fits poorly: it goes into the plan under a rule that restricts access to it, rather than being dropped.
                    In-context observation
                    Free time in natural settings with no prompts: what the student approaches, for how long, and who initiated. Items outside the pool are candidates for the next pool.
                    Competing, partly competing
                    A competing stimulus produces engagement and reduces automatically maintained behavior below its control level: mean engagement ≥ 50% of intervals and a reduction ≥ 80% (partly competing: 50–79%), this form’s conventions.
                    Run This Assessment
                    The panel at the top of each method’s sheet: it keeps the order the sheet uses, times the response window and the access period (or the session), and writes each trial or session into the sheet’s own fields. It never prints.
                    Control sessions
                    In the competing stimulus assessment, two sessions with no items; their mean percentage of intervals with the target behavior is the level each item is compared with.
                    Brief MSWO log and reinforcer-use log
                    The Monitoring sheet’s two logs: the top three of each brief MSWO by date, and each use of an item as a reinforcer, with latency, engagement, rate, rejection and signs.
                    Watch and Shifted
                    Monitoring verdicts: one flag on one item is Watch; two or more flags, or the item out of the top three on two consecutive brief MSWOs, is Shifted.
                    Motivating operation
                    An environmental variable that momentarily alters an item’s effectiveness as a reinforcer (deprivation raises it, satiation lowers it) and the current frequency of the behavior that has produced the item. On the Monitoring sheet: a slow approach after a meal, after free access at home, or late in a long session may be a satiation effect rather than a preference change.
                    Habituation
                    Signs that appear within a session and disappear after a break; vary the item across deliveries, or alternate two items, rather than replacing either.
                    Reinforcer assessment
                    The test of whether a stimulus functions as a reinforcer (RA-1). The hierarchy is a prediction to be confirmed there or in the treatment data.
                    Interobserver agreement
                    Trial by trial for the selection methods, interval by interval for the duration methods and the competing stimulus assessment; at least one session per method, 80% the working minimum, when the hierarchy goes into a plan.
                    Pictorial and verbal formats
                    Pictures or spoken names in place of the objects, only after the prerequisite check: 10 picture–object (or word–object) matching trials in each direction, passed at 90% (working conventions). The pictured item is delivered after each selection. For social stimuli, Kelly et al. (2014) used photos depicting each form of attention, plus a control card that produced no consequence, and checked the resulting hierarchy in a reinforcer assessment.
